Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Press dispatches this morning indicate that President Nasser apparently has not given any assurance that the Suez canal will be open to all shipping once it has been cleared. In view of the fact that the canal is supposed to be opened again a week from Sunday, that is on March 10, this question is becoming very pressing. Apparently there is great concern, for example in Great Britain, as to whether or not the canal is to be open to all ships.
Can the Prime Minister give us the latest information which the Canadian government has on this question and tell us whether there is this probability that the canal will not be open to all ships? Can the Canadian government not take some steps to bring about a situation under which the canal will be open to all shipping?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are a great many rumours, some of them rather contradictory, which are being reported from New York, from Washington and from Cairo at this moment. Our information is only that they are rumours; there will probably be some clarification of the situation after the representative of Israel has made the statement this afternoon for which the deliberations of the United Nations were adjourned until today.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: They don't deal with the canal, do they?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: They do not deal with the canal, but the attitudes of the various parties will, no doubt, be disclosed as a result of what will be taking place after this declaration by Israel. I can assure the hon. gentleman that we are just as anxious as any others could be, though we are not substantial users of the canal, that it should be opened as a seaway for all nations, and it was for that purpose that it was recommended to parliament in the supplementary estimates that an advance be made by us to the United Nations with a view to hastening the clearing of the canal on the understanding that it was to be a seaway open to the trade of all nations without discrimination. We shall continue to do everything within our power to see that this is accomplished, because it appears to us that that is essential to the maintenance of peace in that area-one of the essential conditions for a settlement of the disputes which have caused such anxiety as a result of the happenings of the last several months with respect to the use of the canal and the attitude of the Egyptian government.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could make a few general remarks to hon. members respecting the operation of the Post Office Department before proceeding to the discussion of the estimates for the fiscal year 1957-58.
At the outset may I inform hon. members that the revenue for the fiscal year which ended in 1956 and which appears in the departmental report was $158,568,356. The revenue for the current fiscal year-which can only be an estimate as hon. members will realize because the fiscal year will terminate on March 31-has been estimated at $169,658,000, an increase of slightly over $11 million, or approximately 7 per cent.
I think these figures serve to indicate the increase in the activities and the volume of business of the Post Office Department during recent years. The economic development of Canada of course is of vital concern to the Post Office Department as this department must endeavour to keep in close touch with such development in order to provide the necessary postal services.
The many new problems imposed upon the department as a result of changing trends in industrial and residential areas are being met and have been met through the adoption of new methods of operation and new methods of transportation as well as through the extension of the ordinary postal services.
During recent years there has been a considerable increase in services throughout the country. Letter carrier services in cities have been expanded through the establishment of entirely new services and the extension of existing services, and in the fringe areas of cities where the necessary requirements for letter carrier services have not yet been fully met, a new type of service was instituted a few years ago which is described as the "group box service". This was developed to provide postal patrons with delivery of mail at a central point near their homes, pending the establishment of regular door-to-door services by a letter carrier. During the last fiscal year over 30,000 such group boxes were installed for the service of patrons.
As an illustration of the expansion which has taken place in postal services during the

Supply-Post Office
last year, I think the following statistics may be of interest to hon. members. The increase in the number of letter carrier routes, that is new routes served by letter carriers, has been 217. The increase in the number of rural routes in operation has been 55; the extension of rural routes, 532. The increase in the number of householders served at letter carrier offices was 288,633, while the increase in the number of householders served by rural mail delivery was 21,180. The extension of the services to which I have just referred naturally brought forward the question of the adjustment of compensation to mail contractors particularly those engaged in rural services where, in many cases, it was found the compensation did not meet the present cost of operation. As a result of studies undertaken by the department in recent months, to which I referred a few weeks ago in answer to a question from one hon. member, steps have been taken to rectify this situation. When hon. members refer to the items of the estimates they will see a vote which provides for that.
In the matter of transportation one of the events which, although regrettable, has emphasized the flexibility of the service provided by the post office was the strike of the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway which took place on January 2 and extended to January 13 or 14. On that occasion the department was faced with the problem of organizing alternative mail service for all those points which were normally served by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I must say that I am pleased to be able to report that the personnel of the department were able to meet the challenge. Services were continued for every locality, even points where there were absolutely no road facilities. I feel that this is an indication of the capabilities of the personnel of the department to meet such emergencies, and I was pleased that the comments from both the public and the press were most favourable.
An important development in the transportation of mail has been brought about by the tendency of the railway companies to curtail or cancel completely services on certain lines which they feel cannot be operated economically, or to introduce on some lines a new type of equipment, a diesel car known as the Budd car, which tends to speed up passenger service on an economical basis but does not provide for the volume carriage of mail normally transported. This new policy of the railways has made it necessary for the department to seek other means of transportation. In most cases, as hon. members know, motor vehicle service has been established. Generally speaking, in establishing 
such motor vehicle service to replace curtailed or cancelled trains, the department requires a schedule which provides for the most expeditious dispatch and conveyance of the mails. This has resulted in giving service which is at least as adequate as, and in certain cases an improvement over, service provided in the past.
As hon. members will understand, the expansion in postal services which has been brought about by the rapid growth of this country has brought a multiplicity of management problems in the department. To meet this situation the department has been conducting a training program for the purpose of giving headquarters officers and personnel at the various levels an intimate knowledge of conditions and problems existing in the field service, and also to give personnel in the field service experience at headquarters level. This and other activities in the field of personnel development have not only had the effect of improving the performance of management staff in their present job but have also enabled the department to obtain adequate reserves of personnel who are able to take over increased responsibilities as the demand may arise.
Hon. members will recall that a few years ago the department embarked on a decentralization program, as had been recommended to the department. This has been practically completed throughout the whole service and is working in a very satisfactory manner.
There have also been developments in the international mail services. The exchange of all classes of mail between Canada and other countries is operating on an efficient basis and advantages have been taken of all available, dependent and advantageous opportunities for the dispatch of mail from Canada. There have been more extensions of mail service to other countries, and air parcel post service from Canada now reaches practically all countries of the world. Speaking of international services, I think I should draw to the attention of the committee the meeting of the universal postal union which is to be held in Ottawa as a result of the invitation extended by the Canadian government at the last congress in 1952. This will be the 14th congress of the postal union, and the opening date has been set for August 14 of this year.
I would like to point out that the universal postal union is the oldest international organization of its type in existence. It was established in Berne in 1874. Canada joined the union in 1878. It is an international body which has been accomplishing its work and has been functioning ever since its inception regardless of the political

situation throughout the world. It is an association of countries, having for its object the establishment of a uniform and practical international postal service. The congresses are held every five years, and the delegates of all the member nations, which at the present time number 96, meet in order to revise or complete the acts of the preceding congress as required. The last congress took place in Brussels in 1952, and Canada was signally honoured by being chosen as the place in which the next congress would be held. This is the first time since 1897 that the congress has taken place on the North American continent. It is expected that approximately 350 delegates will be present and the details attendant upon making arrangements for such a congress have for the past three years been receiving the close attention of officers of this department as well as of other departments which may be concerned. It is expected that as usual many proposals will be submitted by the member countries having for their aim the improvement in the exchange of all classes of international mail throughout the world, with resultant benefits for the general public. Just to give an idea of how long and arduous is the work of the congress I might say that at Brussels there were over 1,600 proposals presented for discussion by the delegates.
I said that my remarks would be of a general nature. As usual I shall be pleased to give hon. members all the information I have available on the estimates for the fiscal year 1957-58 which cover the funds which we feel are necessary to keep pace with the developments I have mentioned already. They are based as far as practicable upon forecasts of increased population and the increased use of the mail services by both business and the general public.

Mr. Chairman, I have been listening with a great deal of attention and interest to the statement which has just been made by the Postmaster General and I have noted the detailed information which he kindly supplied about his department.
A moment ago he spoke of the delivery of mail throughout Canada, particularly during the Canadian Pacific railway strike. In all fairness, I must recognize that the employees of the Post Office Department on this inauspicious occasion fully measured up to their responsibilities and that they very

efficiently carried out their duties under particularly trying conditions.
Mr. Chairman, this morning I will have a few general remarks to make, as well as other remarks of more local interest later. In submitting them to the minister's attention, I wish it to be understood that I have in mind the interests of his department as well as the interests of my constituents and of the people of Quebec city where I live.
I wonder if the department would not consider returning to the old system of twice daily mail deliveries. It would mean, I think, a very great improvement, not only for manufacturers, merchants and professional people, but also for the public as a whole. Since the once a day delivery was introduced, mail carriers have had to serve far larger areas. I feel this makes their work that much more difficult, especially if we consider distance, the many stairways they have to climb up and down, and the bad Weather they have to face.
Mr. Chairman, my constituency has some business establishments. Having visited some of these at the time the mail came in, I notice that it arrived around 5 or 5.30 in the afternoon, just before closing time. I think that twice daily mail delivery would constitute a real improvement, and I do not see why the department could not see its way clear to re-establishing this system as soon as possible. After all, the taxpayer now pays more postage and it seems to me that he should obtain an improvement in service at least equivalent to this increase.
I would like now to make a few remarks concerning the new stamp issues which will be sold in the various post offices of this country starting March 7. Judging from the illustrations which have come out they represent Canadian sports or sports activities carried out in Canada. There is one on fishing, another on hunting, a third on skiing-a very popular sport in Canada, particularly in my own province, and finally a fourth which, it seemed to me, represents swimming, I did take a close look at that one and, after putting on my glasses, I thought that it pictured a female swimmer. I will not attempt to comment on her looks because the adjectives which I would be tempted to use would be far from parliamentary. I am all for underlining in this way the role of sports in our country, but I wonder if it would not be possible to issue stamps showing a picture of people who have rendered great service to Canada.

Last year, acting upon the request of the caisses populaires of the province of Quebec, I had the pleasure to request the department to issue a stamp commemorating that great Canadian founder of credit unions, Commander Desjardins. I made this suggestion

which I found excellent-following a large number of requests which had been made to me by the authorities of a great many of these credit unions in my province. For a reason which I cannot discuss because I do not know what it is, the government saw fit to turn down that request.
This year-some one mentioned it in the house early this week-February 22nd marked the golden jubilee of the scout movement and the centenary of Lord Baden-Powell, the distinguished founder of that movement which has done so much in the past and still does so much good among the youth of our country. The scout movement of Canada has reached noteworthy proportions, so much so that the Canadian Scout Association whidh had hardly 15,000 members in 1914 now has more than 200,000 members. I think, Mr. Chairman, that if a stamp was issued with a portrait of Lord Baden-Powell we would pay a respectful and delicate tribute to the memory of a great leader whose initiative and devotion were highly recognized in all countries of the commonwealth.
Mr. Chairman, reverting to a more local matter, may I call upon the minister to do what he can to speed up if possible the negotiations which have been going on for more than a year between authorities of the Canadian National Railways and Quebec city so that the capital of my province might finally obtain its postal terminal, that we have been hearing about for almost three years now. The minister might say that the building of this postal terminal is primarily a responsibility of the Department of Public Works. However, I believe that if the minister brought pressure to bear to hasten the building of that terminal, Canadian National authorities might move a little faster in their negotiations, because they are the ones responsible for the slowness of those negotiations to which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred the other day in reply to a question I had asked.
Mr. Chairman, either the postal terminal is a necessity or it is not. If it is, let us do whatever is required to have it built with the least possible delay.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to speak on behalf of the majority of the people I
[Mr. Dufresne.l
have the honour to represent in this house in requesting from the minister necessary improvements at what is known as the St. Sauveur post office. It now occupies an old building which could be improved considerably or, better still, completely rebuilt along more modern lines. St. Sauveur district, as the minister well knows, comprises seven densely populated parishes and it would only be fair, I believe, to build an adequate and more modern post office there.
I also wish to call the minister's attention to complaints which have been made to me to the effect that some employees of the central post office on Henderson street, in Quebec city, are no longer allowed to use a chair or some kind of a bench while at work. I believe it is particularly in connection with the distribution or sorting of local mail, and I cannot see why these people, who are forced to spend long hours on their feet, could not do this work as well as they did in the past if they were allowed occasionally to sit on a bench or chair.
I would also point out to the minister that it might be a good plan to look into the matter of certain people who are a little lacking in humanity in dealing with subordinate staff.
It seems to me that these faithful public servants should be treated with a little more consideration and not be told, every time they sit down at their work: "Say there, this is not a hospital. If you can't do your work standing up, you had better go home!" All the employees I know perform their task conscientiously and deserve, I think, a better treatment.
I take this opportunity to protest against the dictatorial doings of some authorities whose aim is to curry favour not so much with the minister as with the deputy minister, who seems to forget that before he became deputy minister he was just a minor official. The deputy minister has become a sort of bugaboo with the employees of the Post Office Department throughout Canada, and all of them, except for some of his executive staff, will heave a real sigh of relief and satisfaction the day he will announce the exact date of his retirement. In the interest of the department and of its faithful employees, I hope that he will not be succeeded by one of his understudies, one of his creatures.
In connection with dictatorial doings, I might say a word about the red tape in the

department. Let me give you an example of all the time that is wasted in seijding to the employees letters which, to my mind, are ridiculous. On April 19, 1956-as far as I can make out the date-a Montreal newspaper published a copy of a letter which had been sent to all employees of the Post Office Department. Let me read you this letter. The name is omitted, of course, and you will understand why. I quote:
Your record shows that in the fiscal year 1955-56 you arrived late for work for a total of five rpinutes.
Note the five minutes.
For your own good, as well as for the good of the service, I advise you to take the necessary steps to come to work on time, otherwise you would run the risk of losing part of your annual leave as stated in departmental circular letter No. 399 of May 2, 1955.
Signed: V. M. Chalin For: RENE BOILEAU Postmaster.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the Post Office Department could make better use of its time than writing to employees who certainly have done their duty conscientiously, and upbraiding them, not for a single absence in 365 days, but for having once reported to work five minutes late. As I say, this is ridiculous and mean, and it is high time something were done to avoid recurrence of such nonsense.
While I am on the subject of punctuality and holidays, I want to point out to the minister the unfairness, in respect to which I think he will agree with me, of remunerating overtime done by postal employees (particularly during the holiday rush) by means of additional leave instead of cash. If those employees, most of them family men, are willing to forego their leisure and restful time at home to work overtime, they obviously need to earn a little more than the salary they get.
I do not see why the department should obstinately refuse to pay them at an hourly rate, and force them to take additional leave in payment of their overtime.
Would the hon. minister object to telling us, when closing the debate, if his department has succeeded in negotiating a new contract for letter carriers with the Quebec Power Company, of the city of Quebec?
And now, I would ask the hon. minister to approach the postal authorities of the city of Quebec about letting some 80 residents of a small place along North River, called Boudreau Park, but named St. Sauveur for

I was very much amused the other day, Mr. Chairman, when I asked the hon. minister to try to stop the practice whereby members of this house receive in their postal boxes propaganda which is sent to them almost daily by the Russian Embassy in Ottawa. The hon. minister answered that if the hon. representative from Quebec West would allow him to open his mail he would stop the communications from reaching him. Mr. Chairman, I want to conclude my remarks by telling this house and the hon. minister about an editorial published on July 14, 1956, by Le Reveil, of Ste. Foy, a suburb of Quebec and a prosperous little place, which rightly complains that the Post Office Department has replaced its historic and about a century old name by the designation "Quebec No. 10". I do not see how the delivery can be made easier by a single figure, when it would be quite as convenient to use the name of a town in the suburban area of a larger city. This is what the editorial says:
The name of our city has been changed.
Ste-Foy, parish, town and city, known under that name for hundreds of years, no longer exists.
According to official notices of the Post Office Department, Ste-Foy is no longer in existence.
Its official name is now Quebec 10.
There was a time, not so long ago, when villages and towns were known under the name given to

them by their founders. A name, like Ste-Foy, meant something; it usually had historic connotations; it sometimes recalled a legend, a fact, a great personality or even a humorous occasion. Anyway, that name meant something.
Times have changed.
We are now up-to-date, as they are in "the States".
Quebec 10!
Who ordered this change?
The federal parliament? No!
The provincial parliament? No!
The county council? No!
The city council? No!
A popular referendum? No!
In fact, this change did not originate with any responsible public body; it was made without the public or anybody being consulted. It has simply been ordered by an official of the Post Office Department.
The official reason is no doubt that mail bearing an address such as "Quebec 10" can be handled and delivered faster than mail addressed "Ste-Foy, P.Q.".
If this radical change helped improve to any extent the postal service-not only mail delivery but the whole postal service-it could perhaps be justified but, in fact, the only improvement so far has been to strengthen the monopoly of the Henderson street post office at the expense of local sub-stations.
Ste-Foy, which has now been arbitrarily deprived of its name by the Post Office Department, without even a consultation; Ste-Foy, with a population of 16,000 people, covering an area greater than Quebec city, has not even a suitable post office.
We still have the small post office under the most devoted and competent direction of Miss Laroche, but it is totally inadequate. The premises are far too small, the post office is understaffed and the special services are completely inexistent.
If you wish to enjoy postal privileges for your mail-not a favour but a statutory privilege-you cannot get it by sending your request to the Ste. Foy post office. No. You must go to the Henderson street post office-five miles from the Suete road-where no parking is allowed at any hour of the day. All postal business, other than the purchase of postage stamps, must be dealt with there. And if you are granted privileges to which you are entitled by law, you must deliver the postal items to which such privileges do apply, to the Henderson street post office and nowhere else. Otherwise, your privileges are lost.
In the language of the civil service, this is called "streamlining". But, in everyday language, where words are stronger and carry more meaning, this is simply called an abuse or a lack of the sense of its responsibility toward the taxpaying population on the part of a public department.
Ste-Foy is not the only suburban town affected; our neighbour, Sillery, is not much better off, even though it has a more modern building.
A few years ago, that same Post Office Department at a stroke of the pen crossed out the name of St. Boniface, a small French-Canadian town, near Winnipeg. It was simply decided that from then on that town would be known in postal vernacular, as Winnipeg 6. Fortunately, the French-speaking element, in the provinces where it is a minority, is not dead, far from it; so the department had to reconsider its decision and to find another solution, a very simple one indeed, to the problem of mail distribution. As a matter of fact, the solution is simple; it consists for the Post Office Department in "minding its own business", i.e. the proper delivery of mail entrusted to the "mails of Her Majesty Elizabeth II" in Canada, in receiving this mail and delivering it as addressed and not where the department wishes

it were addressed. The choice of a town's name is no business of the Post Office Department.
It is as simple as that . . .
But if we want it to remain simple, we must not try to "put everything in the same mail bag"; in other words, instead of attempting to enlarge the Henderson street post office to the bursting point, it would be much wiser and more logical to establish local post offices in every suburban town and to give each one of them the responsibilities and facilities which will enable them to serve the public efficiently, swiftly and economically.
(Signed) The Editor.

Mr. Chairman, certainly the C.C.F. is very happy to associate itself with the tribute paid by the minister to the loyalty and efficiency of the postal staff in this country. It is natural I think that most of us should come in touch most frequently with our letter carriers and I know that in Winnipeg whether it be in tropical heat or arctic winter my mail is always delivered promptly. On occasions even for weeks at a time the temperature may descend to 15 or 20 below zero with the wind blowing either from the prairies or from the tundras yet always the letter carrier is on the job performing his duties faithfully and diligently.
But if I have a high regard for the services which are given to us by the staff of the Post Office Department I do not have that same high regard for some of the policies of the department. The minister said in his introductory remarks that the department keeps in close touch with developments in order to provide needed services. That may be so generally but specifically I am prepared to argue that it is not so.
There is in my constituency a municipality which is growing very rapidly and which within a few weeks will become a city because it has applied for a charter. I refer to East Kildonan. The population there in 1946 was some 8,000 souls. Now there are approximately 20,000 human beings resident in that city and in the opinion of those who live there-and they are responsible people who tell me this-the postal services are inadequate.
There are three sub-post offices, two in drugstores and one in a corner store. There is no complaint concerning the quality of

service that is rendered by the people who operate these sub-post offices. There is complaint, however, about the lack of facilities. These people are doing their best but the fact remains that in this rapidly developing municipality new stores, banks and offices are being opened. The answer which was given to me when I pointed this out to the minister was that the revenue which these sub-post offices receive was really not very great and certainly not sufficient to justify a post office being erected there. But again I am informed-and I accept the word of those who tell me this because they know-that a very substantial number of the residents of East Kildonan do not use the postal services there but instead take their mail, parcels and so on down town into Winnipeg. The department tells me that there is a post office in Winnipeg proper, station "F", which is quite near East Kildonan and that is true; it is six blocks away. But this post office serves Elmwood which has a population of approximately 15 or 16 thousand and I am informed it also has to serve East Kildonan with a population of nearly 20,000. If the minister had an opportunity to examine this post office he would realize that the staff has its problems there. The facilities are not at all adequate and furthermore the letter carriers, those people who at times I think do a job far beyond the call of duty, have to depart from station "F" to go into all the corners of East Kildonan, and I am not sure that is a fair thing to ask of these letter carriers. What I am concerned about is getting a proper post office for this burgeoning city of East Kildonan. A question I should like the minister to answer now, if he can, is this. How many cities with a population of 20,000 in this country do not have a post office?

prepared to accept the minister's explanation but nevertheless I am also prepared to say now that I do not believe there are many cities in this country with a population of

Mr. Chairman, strange though it may seem, my purpose in participating in the debate at this time is not to protest, complain or criticize but rather to commend the department for certain developments within my own constituency.
A few years ago, as I recall now, I did have cause to stand here in my place in the house and register some rather severe criticism, most of which, if I recall correctly, related to the inadequacy of the facilities, but fortunately those difficulties have been or are being met.
Possibly I should suggest to the Postmaster General that some of his own members may criticize as a consequence of what I am going to say now. Officials of the department will recall that it was not many years ago that we had a very difficult situation in the city of Red Deer. In 1940 the population was approximately 3,000 and today it is over 14,000. During that time a beautiful building was constructed in the city costing iri excess of a quarter of a million dollars. Then, of course, a door-to-door delivery system was instituted and this took care of that difficult situation. In my own home town of Innisfail they are now in the process of constructing a building the cost of which I presume will run in the neighbourhood of $80,000. In the estimates last year there was $155,000 for a building in Three Hills, and I notice there is another $50,000 in the estimates this year. There was a difficult situation in the town of Olds last year, so I am pleased to find $150,000 in the estimates this year for a public building. It is for this reason I say the minister may, as a consequence of these things, have some difficulty with his own members. While we may not have had more difficult problems than those which existed iri other constituencies, possibly we did put forward a little additional pressure or something of that kind.
I am going to go beyond that and say that the vast improvement which we have en-

Supply-Post Office
joyed in service in that constituency must be attributed in large measure to the personnel of the Post Office Department, plus the fact that a policy was adopted of placing area superintendents iri strategic points. The first area superintendent in the Red Deer area was Mr. Ivor Beams, who is no longer there in that capacity. He was given a well deserved promotion and is now postmaster in the city of Calgary. The area superintendent established a very close liaison between the local postmasters arid between the department and the mail carriers. I feel this was a tremendously important development. Mr. Beams has been succeeded by Mr. J. L. Catley who was in Calgary prior to coming to Red Deer. He is also doing a very excellent job.
I cannot, of course, overlook the district director and his staff in Calgary. May I just point out something that happened very recently. I had cause to write to the postmaster at Red Deer to secure certain information, not about his own office. I got a reply and then wrote to the area superintendent, and got a reply. He in turn got in touch with the district director in Calgary, who in turn got in touch with the director of transport in Ottawa, who in turn got in touch with me. All of this happened within the space of eight days, so one could not complain much about that. I must say that I am extremely pleased to find that that sort of situation exists. I am riot going to suggest that a slight problem might not crop up from time to time, but I do wish to take this opportunity of commending the Post Office Department. If all services within my constituency were operated as satisfactorily as the Post Office Department, perhaps my constituents would decide they did not need me and that would be a rather unhappy development, looking at it from a personal point of view.
I must say also that my Liberal opponent is taking credit for all that has been done. I have simply told the people that if he can do all that has been done they would be foolish to send him to Ottawa; he is too valuable back there. I think probably the people will take my advice in that respect. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I must say I am always pleased to give credit where credit is due. On the other hand, I find it possible to criticize where I think criticism is justified.
I do wish to commend the post office authorities, and I cannot forget the Department of Public Works because, after all, they construct 
the building. My thanks, therefore, are extended to them. They have given us a highly satisfactory type of service in the Red Deer constituency and I know the people are very pleased with what has been done.

Supply-Post Office
area, where there are a million and a hall people, a vast amount of mail is on a local basis. That change has been a great help indeed.
Another point the minister mentioned was a type of service that was instituted last year by the group box service. Hon. members may not know just exactly what it is. It consists of a group of boxes, many people call them green boxes because they are painted green. When you get a new residential subdivision with perhaps two or three hundred houses in it, and which is separated from the normal growth of the area by perhaps a mile or more of empty land which is not built on, they are sort of sitting there in isolated positions. They have all of the normal services of a city such as roads, water, sewers and streets, but because of this isolation they have not door-to-door mail delivery. It is not possible to bring the delivery to them because there is no transportation and because of other factors that may make it very difficult to give them that service. But in the new service the post office provides the boxes and puts them in groups of perhaps 20 or 30. Usually there is just one location, with sometimes two or three on the main road of the subdivision and every householder has a box. The whole thing has a locking system on it. Instead of the people having to go to the local corner store, the drug store or the post office where they have a general delivery system, the mailman simply deposits the mail in the group boxes and when the people return home from work at night, or the children from school, they go to the boxes and pick up the mail. It is an imaginative idea because it fills in the interim period when people just naturally demand a door-to-door delivery and when circumstances are not such that delivery can be instituted.
We have found this system most useful in many parts of my constituency. I might at this time mention to the minister and the department that there will be many more requests in the near future for this type of thing from my constituency.
As I say, it has not all been easy. There are perhaps two or three fields in which some improvement can be made. With great respect I want to put on the record a few recommendations, four to be exact, in regard to changes in procedure and system which might be of some benefit to the department.
The first has to do with the initiation of new mail delivery services. I submit that there should be greater local authority to initiate necessary surveying in order to bring to the attention of the department the need for

new delivery services. Let me explain the present system. The local postmaster, say of Scarborough, knowing the area he is serving, is required to keep his eye on the developments on the fringe of his area and at the appropriate time make recommendations to the postmaster in Toronto who has supervisory authority over all the other local post offices.
He makes a recommendation that an official survey be made of the area concerned. The postmaster in Toronto then communicates with the operations department in Ottawa and requests authority to make such a survey. Authority is given and he has the survey carried out through the local postmaster, in this case the Scarborough postmaster. The survey is prepared and forwarded by the postmaster in Toronto, after he has looked it over, to the operations department in Ottawa. Then they make a decision as to what if any new services will be provided in the area concerned.
As hon. members can understand, there is quite a chain of command involved in this process. There are to some degree delays that occur between the intermediate steps which are taken. My suggestion is that once a pattern of growth is established, such as has occurred in that part of Toronto, the Toronto postmaster should be given authority to tell the local postmaster to prepare surveys. As a matter of fact they could tell the local postmaster to keep a running survey in the form of a chart or map. As the area grows he could simply indicate the increase in the surrounding residential subdivisions so that he could at any time inform the postmaster in Toronto exactly what was occurring in the fringes of his area.
If this were done the postmaster in Toronto, after this had reached a certain point, could transmit the information to the operations department at Ottawa and request that it be reviewed. About one-half of the steps that are now taken could perhaps be eliminated with I think very little extra help being required to keep such a running survey. In an area where you have an established growth pattern such as we have in metro Toronto such a system might prove most beneficial in speeding up the initiation of new door to door services. That is my first recommendation.
My second recommendation has to do with transportation. We see changes occurring in transportation methods in our large cities. At one time you could not get people to live in suburban subdivisions unless there was public transportation available, but that day has passed. We now have expressways and modern highways. Everybody has a car, in fact a tremendous number of people have two cars. You find people living with normal city services out in what would in the past have

been isolated suburban subdivisions, driving their own cars with no public transportation available.
We in metro Toronto have been greatly disappointed in the progress the Toronto transportation commission has made in providing public transportation to these areas. This handicaps the work of the post office because under the present regulations a mail carrier service cannot be provided unless there is some means of getting to the area by public transportation.
I wonder if there is not some way by which the Post Office Department could provide alternative methods of transportation in order to get their mail delivery men into these areas. It is my understanding that under the present regulations a man cannot use his own car, and perhaps this could be looked at. Perhaps mail delivery men could be found who would provide their own transportation for which they would be recompensed. Perhaps it would be possible for the local post office where such service is required to have some sort of trucking service by which the postmen could be taken in to the area and brought out at the proper time, or perhaps mail delivery men could live in the area and their mail be taken in and dropped at a point for them to pick it up.
I submit the thinking of the department will have to turn in that direction. Perhaps my suggestions have not been too comprehensive in that regard, but I am concerned with this change that has occurred in transportation methods. I would urge the department to consider modifying the regulations to provide for other means of transportation than public transportation for the mail carriers where required. That is my second recommendation.
My third recommendation has to do with co-operation between the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works in regard to the construction of new buildings. It is quite a lengthy procedure to make arrangements for the construction of a new post office building. It is necessary first to find a site, and in a fast-growing area that is not easy. In fact, sometimes that is the most difficult part of the whole process. Once a site is chosen it has to be purchased and the legal procedures necessary to get title carried through. Then proper surveys must be made so that a building can be designed of the right size to handle not only the present needs but the future needs. Then the building has to be tendered for and erected.
We found considerable difficulty in getting through these procedures in connection with the construction of our Scarborough post
Supply-Post Office
office. Fortunately the department was able to acquire temporary quarters in which they could provide service before the new building was completed. That permitted the department to take a little more time in planning for the new building. The department may be surprised to know that this building in Scarborough which has just been completed is now packed to the limit. I visited it the other day and found that with the institution of some of the new services we hope to get the officials will be hard put to find space in which to continue the operations.
Fortunately the building was constructed in such a manner that the back wall can be knocked out and an addition erected. It is indicative of the growth of that area that most of the public buildings, not just the post office but the schools and everything else, are constructed in this manner so that changes can be made. However, I would recommend and request, Mr. Chairman, that there should be closer contact between the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works in order to speed up the processes which must necessarily be gone through and to have these buildings constructed more expeditiously. I think that is a matter to which it would be beneficial for both departments to give some thought. That is my third recommendation.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to mention post office salaries. I have a schedule of salaries here, not, of course, for the whole post office system but for postmasters in Scarborough and other towns, postal clerks, sorters, wicket clerks and letter carriers. A letter carrier begins at a salary of $2,640 a year and after four years reaches a maximum of $3,360. Postal clerks start at $2,640 and after six years can reach $3,660. I simply do not know, Mr. Chairman, how a married man raising a family can exist on $2,640 a year, and I do not know how he can look forward with any great anticipation to a maximum of $3,360 or $3,660, for that matter, after four or six years of work.
I know it is not possible to divorce salaries paid to postal clerks and postmasters from the general level of the salaries paid throughout the civil service. That is a matter for the civil service commission. And yet I think there should be greater flexibility in the system used. I have to pay a good legal secretary at least $60 a week, even to start, in order to get anyone in Toronto. That works out around $3,100 a year. Yet here we have postal clerks and letter carriers who have the responsibility of dealing with your mail and mine who are working hard, and starting at $2,640 in both cases. I do urge the department to take a hard look at these salaries to see if something cannot be done to provide a better

Supply-Post Office
income for these people. At $3,360 a year a letter carrier can hardly qualify under the National Housing Act to purchase a house in which to make a home. This may not be too comprehensive an argument, but it is at least an illustration that there are civil servants at the present time who do not have the salary qualification necessary before they can take advantage of federal legislation which was presumably passed for the benefit of every Canadian.
I see that the salary for the postmaster at Scarborough has a starting rate of $5,040. A postmaster in a post office such as Scarborough has 37 letter carriers to supervise; he has all the necessary sorters and wicket clerks to look after, in addition to his deputies, yet with all this responsibility he is starting off at $5,000 a year. Why, a man doing a similar job in private business would be earning at least $10,000; you would not get a good man to do the job for less.
It is true that there are other benefits in the civil service which are not found in private business, but I think it is high time we took another look at these salaries and tried to do something about it.
Well, Mr. Chairman, those are my four recommendations. As the minister has said, this is a question of the post office keeping abreast of the economic development of our country and providing the necessary services to go along with it. I must say I have been pleased with the effort put forth in this riding of York-Scarborough, which is the most populous riding in Canada-
