Mr. Chairman, a little change was made in the mail service in my riding 82715-1144
Supply-Post Office
last year. The post office decided they were going to truck the mail up in that end of the country, and it was taken off the trains. At that time we tried our best to persuade them to leave it the way it was, but the Post Office Department claimed that the railway had given them notice that no more mail would be carried on the trains. I went to the Post Office Department about it, but they said it was out of their hands and that they had to find some other way of transporting the mail. Trucks were hired, and the mail in that section of the country is now delivered by truck.
I know as well as the Post Office Department knows what the answer is going to be in about another hour. Nothing has been done yet and it is no use to holler before we are hurt. The inference is simply this. They intended to take off some of the train services. As long as the mail was carried on the trains they could not do it very graciously, so they took another way around.
I want to tell them that the service is not any better because we are getting delivery by truck. As a matter of fact, in my own case there have been two or three instances when it took two or three days to get a letter from one side of the county to the other. That has not always happened; in the same period I have had letters from the same place in 24 hours. I do not know whose fault it is; it could be a slip on somebody's part. I would not blame it entirely on the Post Office Department; it is just one of those things that happen, and we are not very well satisfied with it. We were not very well satisfied with the trucks delivering the mail.
I would like to say a word about the rural mail carriers. I am in full agreement with the Post Office Department that these men should have salary increases. For some years many of these fellows have worked very hard and have received very little remuneration for their work. That was not altogether the fault of the Post Office Department; it was the fault of the applicant who bid too low in the first place, who got the contract and then found he could not make any money. The Post Office Department came to his rescue and, as is very often done, raised the rate of remuneration. I see now that the rates are going to be raised again.
I see nothing wrong with that, as I believe a man should be worthy of his hire. The mail carrier is a little better class of man than the ordinary rank and file. He must be honest, he must have a certain amount of prestige, he must have backers so that if he does go off the deep end there will be some way of getting back at him. He is a little better calibre of man than the ordinary

Supply-Post Office
worker, and for that reason he deserves better wages. Therefore I am in agreement with increasing their remuneration.
Something was said about abuses of the franking privilege. I believe this does take place, though I am not one of those who are guilty. There is a lot of franking done that should not be allowed, and this is not confined to any one part of the house. It is necessary that we have franking privileges because we do not make anything from the mail we send out. It is a privilege I enjoy and I do not abuse it, and I do not think anyone else should.
I should like to ask the minister two or three questions. I was one of those who did not think it was necessary to raise the postage rate from 4 to 5 cents, and I should like the minister to tell us what revenue was obtained by the Post Office Department because of that increase. 1 should like the minister to tell the committee if any money was advanced by the Post Office Department to other departments of government at the end of the fiscal year. If so, will he indicate to what departments, and the amounts in each case?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few general remarks with regard to the estimates before us. I am glad to see that the department is showing a comfortable margin of profit on its operations. I am one of those who believe it should stand on its own feet, and that the returns from the service provided for the people should take care of the cost of operation. I have been looking over the list of employees, and I note that the largest increase is in city and rural mail carriers. This is as it should be, because with our growing population not only our suburban dwellers but our rural dwellers as well should be provided with adequate mail service.
Another thing I noted in going over the general estimates is that there are still a large number of employees who are pitiably underpaid. Before any consideration is given tb reducing the postal rates, which some people seem to think are too high, consideration should be given to increasing the salaries of the lower paid employees, especially those receiving under $3,600.
I should like to make a few remarks about the service in my own district. First, I back up wholeheartedly the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, who has asked that consideration be given to providing air transportation of mail from Penticton north. I know that this is being talked of and is something that may not come into being in the immediate future, but I ask the officials to keep their eyes on the matter.

I am not too well acquainted with the situation at Summerland, but I have heard complaints from people in the northern part of the Okanagan valley about the mail service they are receiving. I would stress, as did the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, that these matters should receive special consideration.
Looking back over the four years I have been here I must say that I have been pleased with the reception I have received at all times from the officials of the Post Office Department. I have had some complaints, and where necessary I have taken them to the deputy minister. I have never yet found myself forced to go to the minister. I believe in working on these things from the bottom up. A great number of the complaints were solved after they had been placed before the district superintendent. Right here let me say that the setting up of district superintendents is one of the finest things the department has done in the way of streamlining the service or providing liaison between the users of the mails and the Post Office Department. Mr. Stanley, the representative at Kamloops, is doing a wonderful job. He is on the spot, and any complaints that arise are given careful and serious consideration. They are talked over and as a rule are settled on the spot.
During the past four years new post offices have been opened in Enderby, Sicamous and Lurnby, and of course there is the new federal building in Vernon which is still under construction. I am sorry to learn that weather conditions in the Okanagan have not been quite as good this year as we usually expect, and there has been some slow-down. However, it is anticipated that this building will be completed before cold weather comes around again, and then our post office will be housed in one of the finest buildings in the interior of the province. I might mention that I was present last summer when the Minister of Fisheries so well and truly laid the cornerstone of this fine building.
We have had some troubles in the area, but they have not been serious and they have been pretty well ironed out. Many of the complaints were caused by the confusion created by a new mail delivery service put into effect in the area. When the rail service over the branch line from Sicamous down through the valley was discontinued, arrangements were made to carry the mail by truck from Kamloops. There was nothing wrong with the truck service, but at times the users of the postal service were greatly dissatisfied when the truck driver was not able to get the mail to the appointed places on schedule. Quite often they did not take into account

the fact that even the train had been held up by slides or other conditions beyond its control.
I am glad to note that another improvement for which we have asked repeatedly has been brought about. This was talked over with Mr. Stanley, the superintendent of the area, and was finally put into operation. I refer to the combined plane and train service from Vancouver to Penticton. Now mail for the interior, instead of coming from Kamloops, comes to Penticton and then is delivered northward to the main points in the district, from which points the local carriers make their deliveries in trucks.
During the past few years I have noted an increase in rural deliveries. We do not have daily service such as is provided in many districts, but taking it by and large I am satisfied that the people in the riding I represent are getting fairly good service. In the more thickly populated parts of the province rural deliveries are on a daily basis, and we cannot hope for anything more than that.
I cannot speak too highly of the co-operation we have received. There are still two or three things which we must iron out. One of the things that is causing dissatisfaction at the present time is that although a certain part of an area adjacent to Vernon has its own post office, and a very good post office too, the rural carriers are working out of Lumby, while at the present time a large part of that district is served by a route from Vernon. I do not think that is fair to the business people of Lumby, and I am looking forward to the time when that will be changed.
We cannot expect to have foolproof results from the Post Office Department, of course, any more than we can expect to obtain them from any department in which the human element plays such a large part. There are cases, of course, where letters are not delivered as promptly as we think they should be, but on the other hand there is usually some good reason for non-delivery, and we must admit that sometimes it might be due to the carelessness of a local employee which cannot be provided for.
There is one other thing I would like to mention. Despite the improvements in the greater part of our district we still have a little problem in the east end. We are not too far from Revelstoke or even from Sica-mous, but we are cut off from them, and letters have to travel hundreds of miles under the present arrangements in order to reach a town which may be only 25 miles away. I do not know what the solution would be, but it is not a big problem, and looking at the picture generally I recognize that we
Supply-Post Office
must, of course, always consider the service given to the greatest number. However, there is a little problem there which I think we can continue to work on, and I am sure we shall be able to find a solution without bringing it up before the minister in charge of this department.
In concluding I join with those who have commended the service and co-operation we have received and are receiving, and say we are satisfied that action is being taken to improve the services the post office is giving, and that we are satisfied it is the policy of the department to try to continue to improve that service.

Mr. Chairman, there are a number of questions I would like to ask the minister subsequently, in order that he might reply to them together with other points which have been raised in this discussion, but I would like to make a few general remarks first.
The minister has heard, and rightly so, praise and commendation from all parts of the house this afternoon for certain aspects of the operations of his department, and more specifically for the efforts put forward by the mass of the employees in the Post Office Department whose number totals, if I remember rightly, some 50,000. That is as it should be. These are hard-working, conscientious people who are giving devoted service to their country. They are handling nearly four billion pieces of mail a year, and I join with other hon. members in commending them for their devotion and hard work.
Let me say this, Mr. Chairman. I hope the Postmaster General will not be led by that into rising subsequently and saying, "You have said so many nice things about my employees that those of you who have made certain critical observations are just unreasonable, carping critics who are contradicting themselves and contradicting other people within the party." Praise for the staff of the Post Office Department and for their efforts does not necessarily include praise for the policies of the department, the expenditures of the department or certain of its actions, and I think that point should be made so we do not have any misunderstanding.
For example, the devotion of the employees of the department is on a full-time basis, and I want to express my regret that a similar practice is not followed by the Postmaster General who, whatever his love for the department may be, finds it necessary to divide his time between two departments. When you are doing a part-time job you cannot be as effective and as efficient as if you are doing a full-time job, and we have reached the point at which the Postmaster

Supply-Post Office
General is without knowledge of what is going on in his own department. I will give only one example, Mr. Chairman, because time is getting short.
I want to point out something that happened here in this house during the last month. On Wednesday, January 23 of this year we find in the Ottawa Journal on the front page a subheading saying, "Twice a Day Mail Delivery Also Being Envisaged." Together with that is the statement:
The government Is considering the restoration of twice a day mail delivery. . . .
And underneath are the words:
Prime Minister St. Laurent today made these disclosures.
There follow some other words which do not affect what I have read. Later on-and I mention this in passing-the Prime Minister is reported in these words:
While he thought the Canadian was some better than the U.S. mail delivery service, there remained ample room for improvement.
So the restoration of two a day delivery was now under consideration.
Then we turn to Hansard for February 6, which is about two weeks later, where we find the hon. member for Peterborough saying at page 1017:
Has any further consideration been given to renewing the twice a day mail delivery ... as was formerly the practice?
Then there are a few more words which do not alter the sense. The Postmaster General replied, "No, Mr. Speaker." Later I asked the Prime Minister a supplementary question, and the Prime Minister again confirmed his previous statement to the press by saying that consideration was being given to the costs that would be involved in respect to a twice a day mail delivery. So I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it would be an excellent thing if we had a full-time postmaster, one who would keep abreast of the major policy developments in his department which are under discussion at cabinet level.
Having said that, I would like to refer to certain observations which the Postmaster General made in the course of his opening statement earlier today. First of all, there is certain information which causes us to consider seriously whether letter carriers are not just being given a heavier and heavier load of households to cover all the time.
Earlier this afternoon an hon. member spoke in terms of 350 houses on a given route. In the estimates committee last year the information was given that the average is 500 households to a route. At that time it was suggested that there would be some variation between 400 and 600, but that

certainly if the figure went over that there was ample cause for investigation and consideration. In his statement today the Postmaster General pointed out that 217 new routes had been established, and he told us that the actual increase in the number of households served was some 288,633. If we take the 217 new routes established and an average of 500 households per route that produces over 103,500 households and leaves the remainder of the increase, 288,633 less 103,500, to be spread over the existing number of letter carriers. In other words, by doing quick addition we find that some 185,000 additional households are being served by the existing number of letter carriers.
Someone may come back at me and say oh yes, but we are splitting these routes and adding new letter carriers. Before that observation is made I would point out that the estimates of the department for 1956-57, the same period to which my previous figures refer, provide for an increase in the number of letter carriers from 4,445 to 4,659, which is within about 10 of the number of new routes that have been established.
There is no doubt whatsoever from the evidence before us that the letter carriers are being asked more and more to handle heavier burdens. I need only say that in the city of Montreal right now there are routes running between 800 and 900 households. I think that is a conservative figure. I have heard some people complain of as many as 1,100, but I find it quite impossible to accept that figure. Certainly there are many routes in excess of the average, and that applies right across the country. I think there should be some explanation of what is happening in that regard.
I now turn to another piece of information in the minister's statement. He referred to the universal postal union which is to meet here in August of this year, I believe. I agree with him that it is a signal honour for Canada that the meeting should be held here, and I think we will all welcome the 350 delegates who are coming to the meeting. But, Mr. Chairman, welcome as they are, much as we want them to enjoy themselves, is it necessary for us to expend $250,000 of the public's money in order to provide facilities for the convention? That works out to $800 a delegate. In addition, last year $25,000 was spent in preparing for it, and previously there had been a few thousand odd dollars. That works out to more than $800 for every one of the 350 delegates.
I do not think there is a person in the house who has been to a convention, certainly no one who has run one, who knows of a Canadian convention which operates

on the basis of putting up expenses averaging $800 per person or a total, as I have said, of $250,000. Let us remember that these people are paying their own travelling expenses and are looking after themselves while here. This amount is for convention facilities. It is the grandest, most expensive welcome and the most expensive convention I have ever heard of. I do not quite know on what the money is going to be spent, but I hope we will have a very detailed explanation from the minister by the time he is through.
Maybe they are going across the river to Hull.

Someone suggests they may be going across the river to Hull. I know that things are somewhat more expensive in the province of Quebec, but unless a special hotel is going to be built for them with gold-plated fixtures I find it difficult to imagine on what the money is going to be spent. I hope the minister will have an explanation.
I turn now for a moment to the question of twice a day mail service. Let me say immediately that there is no quarrel with the rural areas in their demand for a minimum delivery once a day, nor is there any doubt in the mind of any of us, I think, that certain areas now on rural routes or on box systems are entitled to twice a day delivery. The point I would make is that the elimination of twice a day mail delivery service has caused and is continuing to cause considerable distress and inconvenience in our metropolitan areas that are now served by letter carrier service.' The costs were worked out in detail and presented to the estimates committee last year. They represented approximately one-third of the surplus of the Post Office Department for the year 1955-56, and they will represent less than one-half of the estimated surplus of the Post Office Department for the current year. In other words, we could change to twice a day delivery service, five days a week, and still leave the Post Office Department with a substantial surplus. When the minister replies I hope he will tell us what the situation is with regard to the resumption of twice a day mail delivery.
I point out to the minister that in some respects his department is very slow administratively. For example, let me take the Christmas overtime payments. Remember that Christmas came as always on the 25th of December. We have reached the first of March, and if the employees in the Montreal area have received their Christmas overtime remuneration certainly it has only been within the last few days because prior
Supply-Post Office
to that, whatever the reason may be, the money had not been disbursed to a great many of the employees.
Furthermore, I think it is unfortunate that the Post Office Department seems inclined to take a chance and break other rules and regulations of the government. We all know there is a requirement that salaried employees be advised by the end of February regarding the remuneration they received in the previous year. Last year we showed that the department had not done that. They were so slow in preparing the information that it was after the end of February before the employees received the information as to their remuneration, and that was a direct contravention of one of the income tax regulations.
We are so close to the breaking point, March 1, at this moment that I am not in a position to say that the same situation applies this year. But this I do know, that up to three or four days ago, when I last had the opportunity to check, this information had not gone out to the employees in the Montreal area. It may have gone out in Toronto but had not gone out in the Montreal area, and it rather looks as if one department is again contravening the regulations made by another.
In order to be fair and give the minister the opportunity to reply before five o'clock, when we proceed to take up private bills, I am going to reserve the rest of my remarks for the first item or more appropriate items later on. But I would say to the minister, quite apart from the points that have been raised, that I felt his statement this morning -considering that it was the statement of someone coming to this house to report on behalf of a department which affects every Canadian-was pallid, innocuous and devoid of almost all the information one would have expected to be supplied to this house.
Let me touch just on a few of the items. The department is deeply involved in the development of a new electronic mail sorting machine and the costs are now running at something over $1 million; not a word about that. The civil service commission was supposed to be studying the classification of postmasters in order to arrive at a standard formula by which postmasters could be classified as to grade; not a word about that. Over the last year the department has embarked on an extended program involving the use of stamp vending machines across the country in public places; not a word about that.
The department has been questioned year after year with respect to the number of robberies and break-ins at post offices, which is a source of considerable irritation and results in considerable sums of money being lost; not

Supply-Post Office
a word about that. The department has been meeting a considerable problem in the field of mail transportation due to the extension of the use of new types of aircraft such as the Viscount, the mail carrying capacity of which is substantially less than in the case of the aircraft previously used. What steps are being taken to meet that problem? We do not know because there was no mention of this in the minister's statement.
And perhaps most interesting of all, in the estimates committee last year we were told that the department was just on the verge of having some very complete information regarding their operations, the cost by classifications of mail and the breakdown of their revenues through the establishment of a cost ascertainment division, the first studies of which were to be ready in September, 1956. This is information which is of tremendous importance, because it opens up a whole new vista in the subject of the Post Office Department. Yet the Postmaster General did not see fit in his remarks to make any reference whatever to the information which has been obtained in this way or to what progress has been made in respect of these studies.
These are great gaps, Mr. Chairman; and knowing something about the operation of the Post Office Department, because it affects every Canadian, we on this side of the house are in a position to take up these questions and delve into the operations of the department and ask the minister questions, and we shall do so. I would suggest to the minister, however, that it would be preferable for him to realize that when he comes into this house to make an initial statement it would be helpful to every one of us if he would avoid banal generalities and give us a really adequate review of the operations of his department.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make and I shall be brief, because I realize the minister is perhaps expecting to make some reply before five o'clock.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat and many others who have taken part in this debate have recommended that there should be two mail deliveries daily in the cities and urban centres where that type of service was previously provided. I for one would strongly suggest to the minister that before any consideration is given to increasing the service in cities and urban areas from one to two deliveries daily he should use his influence and first see to it that other citizens in this country and particularly those in the rural areas have at least one delivery a day.
In my own county there are several rural mail routes where they have three deliveries

a week, and with respect to one route they have four deliveries a week. I believe these citizens have every right to expect a daily mail delivery before two deliveries daily are made possible for other citizens in this country.
For those who enjoy receiving a daily newspaper it is a great inconvenience to receive that newspaper the day after it is published. My constituents bring this matter to my attention quite often, and I believe it is only fair to say they should have first consideration. In order to provide two deliveries daily in our cities it would mean a great expense for the department. Again I noticed that those in the official opposition were not hesitant about suggesting additional expenditure, but that is to be expected.
If we hope to give an eight-hour day to the employees of the Post Office Department, which they have every right to expect along with other civil servants, it means that we must employ a great many additional people in post offices right across Canada. I know that in my own home town, which is rather small, in order for the Post Office employees to be given a five-day week it was necessary to increase the staff, and it must certainly be an expensive procedure to follow in the larger cities.
Before improving the service in the cities and towns to the point where everyone is happy, I hope the minister will give serious consideration to those citizens who live in rural areas and who now have three or four mail deliveries a week. They would very much appreciate having a daily mail delivery. I know he will give this matter serious consideration, and we look forward to the time when we will all be having at least one mail delivery a day.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that my reaction to the question of the twice a day mail delivery service is very similar to that of the hon. member for Charlotte. I suppose our thinking in respect to this matter is inclined to be coloured somewhat by the type of constituency we represent.
As I listened to the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace I came to the conclusion that . I would suggest to the Postmaster General in any consideration he is giving to twice a day mail delivery not to lose sight of the many thousands of people across this country who hope that some day they will have a twice a week mail delivery. As the Postmaster General will readily recognize, the coastal area of British Columbia, a large part of which lies in the Comox-Alberni constituency, is one of the most difficult areas in Canada for the gathering and distribution of mail. There are a great many problems that

arise from time to time in that area, partly because of the nature of the country itself and the manner in which the communities are separated one from another.
I have found, as have some hon. members who spoke today, that most of the problems which come to our attention from time to time relating to this department can be discussed with the district officers of the department and successfully resolved. I must say that as far as my own experience goes, most of the problems which have come to me have been resolved in that manner and there have not been many occasions when I have had to bother the headquarters officers of the department or the minister himself on postal matters. Like the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, I have felt that the move toward the establishment of area superintendents is working out very well.
However, there are some matters which cannot be settled by the officers at the district level. There are one or two problems in my area at the present time upon which I should like to speak briefly. The gist of my remarks at this time is that I should like to seek the assistance of the Postmaster General in some negotiations I have been having from time to time with his colleague the Minister of Public Works. These negotiations relate to the need for improvement in some of the facilities in which some of the employees of the department are going to work, as well as improvements in facilities required by the patrons of post offices. There are a couple of areas in my district where very rapid expansion has been taking place, where the amount of money that is being spent in industrial investments, principally in the pulp and paper industry, is measured in the tens of millions of dollars per annum, and where there has been a consequent rapid increase in population. I feel that early action is required on these problems.
I am referring particularly to the village of Campbell River, the city of Alberni and Port Alberni. I wish the minister could have been with me when I called to see the postmaster in Campbell River not too long before the usual Christmas rush was expected this year. His department has been operating in rented quarters which were leased by the department at a time when Campbell River consisted of nothing much more than a fishing resort village, with a little logging activity. The pressure upon the accommodation there has grown to the point where the postmaster has become really desperate in attempting to secure temporary quarters to handle the Christmas 82715-115
Supply-Post Office
mail, and where the provision of even ordinary day to day mail service has become very difficult.
This Christmas a large part of the staff in the city of Alberni had to work downstairs in an almost unheated basement, with a low ceiling and a concrete floor. Patrons of the post office who wanted to get parcels and general mail delivery were forced to go down a rather narrow, crowded set of stairs. In Port Alberni the post office building is old, being of about first world war vintage, and has long been inadequate to meet the requirements of that area. A number of years ago postal walk service was inaugurated in Port Alberni, and this service has been carried on from an old garage. From the point of view of the welfare of the employees of the department in that area as well as from the point of view of the physical possibility of maintaining adequate service, I hope the Postmaster General will see fit to lend his support to an early construction program in the areas I have mentioned.
During the period to which I have been referring, a new, modern hospital has been constructed in the Alberni valley area, a new hospital is now under construction in Campbell River, and there have been quite a large number of fine new school buildings erected, although they have been having difficulty keeping pace with the demand for school rooms. The facilities in which this important public service has had to operate have not been expanded at all, and I feel that the time has come now when this situation should be met.

The hon. member for Royal expressed the fear that the maritimes might be overlooked in the issuing of these commemorative stamps. In order to allay that fear, I should like to say that the Nova Scotia historical society, as well as my colleague, have asked the Post Office Department for approval of a stamp commemorating the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Nova Scotia house of assembly. We hope the minister and his officials will give this matter favourable consideration in the near future. Nova Scotia was the first province to have responsible government and it was also the first province to have many other things, such as a Joseph Howe who had the strength to stand up and fight for what he thought the maritimes needed.
At this time we are not asking for anything special from the Post Office Department, except that in the near future we would ask for a full review of rural mail contracts. These rural mail carriers are a class of people who operate under great difficulty. They have to be out in all kinds of weather and in Nova

Supply-Post Office
Scotia, as in some other parts of Canada, they still have to travel over dirt roads in some parts of their routes. The cost of everything is going up, including gasoline. Recently we have seen the announcement of an increase in the gasoline tax in Ontario. In Nova Scotia we have the highest gasoline tax of any province in Canada. If the department will give this matter consideration I am sure they will receive support, because everyone feels that the time has arrived when these contracts should be reviewed.
As I said, the Halifax members are not asking for anything in particular. However, we do want to give commendation and praise to the Post Office Department, the officials here in Ottawa and the local officials. I believe the public should be aware that post office officials from the postmaster down to the man who collects and delivers the mail are in positions of trust. I was hoping the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace would join all the others who have been speaking today in such kindly terms about the post office officials. It seemed to me that his was the only dissenting voice we heard today. Perhaps he will have to admit that, for the most part, the service has been excellent.
Certainly we have our little troubles in Nova Scotia, but there are none which cannot be surmounted. There are some specific things for which we should thank the department. Some of them may be small, but all the same they seem important to the people. One of them is the clock in the Dartmouth post office. This clock seemed to be very important to the people in Dartmouth, though I said to them on one occasion that I did not know why they needed it repaired because the only time they used it was when they were going to Halifax.
While we are on Dartmouth, perhaps the Dartmouth post office itself might be looked at. The employees are working under very cramped conditions, which may slow up deliveries. Dartmouth is quite a centre today. As I said a while ago, it is the fastest growing town in Canada and has reached the city stage. They need a very extensive addition to the building, or a new one. For the information of the minister I might tell him he may already possess the information that there is land alongside the present building which is owned by the town of Dartmouth, and I am sure they would co-operate with the department in selling this land at a reasonable price. Perhaps the government would consider moving one of its departments from that building and erecting a building for the particular service which is now using it, namely the unemployment insurance commission. There are several other small things but I am

sure that my colleague and I can deal with them by interviewing the heads of the several departments.
Before I sit down I think I should pay a special tribute to the postmaster in Halifax, his staff and the district superintendent of Nova Scotia, who are always prepared to give good service.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the Postmaster General when he replies would explain the degree of responsibility the department assumes for postal service to the armed forces. I have had certain complaints brought to my attention regarding the slow delivery of service mail. Strange to say, those complaints have not arisen from the forces overseas but from the forces stationed in some of the large encampments here in Canada. I do not know whether the Post Office Department' itself delivers the mail to those encampments such as Shilo and such as Gagetown will be, but there does seem to be more delay in delivering mail to those service establishments than there is to the nearby towns. I would suggest that service to the armed forces requires looking into.
There is also one particular matter I wish to bring up dealing with the relationship between the Post Office Department and the services, and that is the construction and maintenance of post offices in those various service establishments. I cite a particular case. There is a large number of service houses just outside Victoria at a place which is generally known as Belmont park. Belmont park is located at the entrance to the triservices college at Royal Roads, which is regarded as one of the show places of the Department of National Defence. Visitors from all over Canada go there on graduation days to see the closing exercises. They pass through Belmont park and just before they enter, or just after they pass through the lodge gate going down to the tri-services college, they see a sign reading "post office". That sign is located near one of the contractor's shacks which was left there during the housing construction which was undertaken some five or six years ago. It is the most dilapidated building in the whole of that area.
When I took the matter up with the Department of National Defence they told me that it was the responsibility of the Post Office Department. When I refer to the Post Office Department I am told that it is a matter for national defence, and when I refer to the Minister of Public Works he turns around and says, "I cannot get either the Department of National Defence or the Post Office Department to come to an agreement over this building, and I cannot start to put up anything which is suitable and which conforms with the

buildings in the area until those two departments come to an agreement".
Now, I am not exaggerating when I say it is nothing but a dilapidated, unattractive shack. A car ran into it a couple of years ago and broke in the side of the building. No water is provided for the staff; and outside of the disgraceful appearance of the building, which is put at an angle to all the other buildings, it is impossible for the staff to provide the service which the patrons of that area have a right to expect. Furthermore, there is the question of the security of the mail. A good deal of service mail and a good deal of other important mail goes through that office because some of the families are the families of sailors who are at sea during a considerable period of their time, and I can assure you that when the serviceman is away-and mail can only come in occasionally, when the ship he is serving on happens to visit a port-the letters are regarded as something very precious.
I feel that for the security of Her Majesty's mail, for the accommodation of the staff, for the convenience of the patrons and the general appearance of the area and the impression which is made on the large number of visitors going to the tri-services college, something better should be provided. I would really like to know where the responsibility lies. Is it with the Postmaster General, is it with the Minister of National Defence or is it the Minister of Public Works who just will not get on with the job? I am inclined to think it is not the Minister of Public Works, although he is looking at me. I believe if he were told to go ahead and provide suitable accommodation he would get ahead with it. Therefore I suggest that the Postmaster General and the Minister of National Defence get together and remedy this disgraceful situation at the earliest possible opportunity.

Counsel, you are almost putting words into her mouth so I think you had better be careful.

With regard to the passing of these bills, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I believe the other place is now doing a much more thorough job than has been the case heretofore. I rise mainly to take exception to what has been said in certain quarters, namely that hon. members of this house rose to protest these bills merely in order to get their names in the papers. Nothing is farther from the truth. Hon. members of this group opposed the manner in which these cases have been going through the house, and their opposition to divorce bills has, in a number of cases, been strengthened by the fact that we have been able to point out instances where gross injustice was being done. Through contesting certain cases we have brought to the attention of hon. members of this house, as well as to others, the fact that there have been gross injustices which, in my view, were a reflection on parliament.
It was because we believed this manner of granting divorces to be a reflection on this house that we objected to certain of these bills, and I want to say how deeply we resent the insinuation that we have only been doing this for publicity purposes. We have been able to prevent a number of divorces being granted with, I think, the general support of the Canadian people. Some of the evidence which was given was quite openly and quite admittedly perjured. The system and manner in which the evidence in some of these divorce cases was being found was a disgrace to any court in Canada, and certainly a situation which we as Canadians could not continue to permit.
I believe that as a result of our action there has been some improvement in the handling of the cases. And I believe that a number of cases which heretofore, might possibly have come before this house, and which would have gone through this house.

I think this is one of the cases where the type of evidence we have heretofore had presented to the house has been prohibited and a new approach and I think, a much better one, made. The evidence in this case has been presented to the committee, and it is not our intention to try to fight the case or talk it out. But I do think there is evidence that good work is being done. the second reading of Bill No. 105, to incorporate Alaska-Yukon Pipelines Ltd.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to incorporate a pipe-line company under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. As hon. members know, this step is necessary before any company can engage in the operation of a pipe line which crosses a provincial or international border; it must be incorporated by an act of parliament pursuant to the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. It is also necessary to refer the project subsequently to the board of transport commissioners.
The measure now before the house follows the general pattern of pipe-line bills already approved by parliament, and I can assure hon. members that when this particular bill is passed it will not be a dormant measure. The important clause of the bill is probably clause 5, which reads:
The company shall have all the powers, privileges and immunities conferred by, and be subject to all the limitations, liabilities and provisions of the Pipe Lines Act, and any other general legislation relating to pipe lines enacted by parliament with respect to the transmission and transportation of gas and oil and other liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons.
The chief operative part of the bill is clause 6, which empowers the company to construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and operate lines of pipe within Canada, namely in the Yukon Territory, the Northwest Territories and in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia as well as outside Canada. This "outside Canada" provision is necessary because it is planned immediately to construct a 6-inch pipe line from Haines, Alaska, at tidewater on Lynn

canal through Alaskan territory a distance of 40 miles to Pleasant Camp, British Columbia; thence a 4^-inch pipe line approximately 119 miles through the northwest tip of British Columbia to Haines Junction in Yukon Territory, to connect with the existing Canol system of pipe lines at that point.
The company plans to build this pipe line, commencing early in May, from the refinery to be constructed at Haines, Alaska, to Haines Junction in the Yukon Territory, a total distance of approximately 159 miles, at an estimated cost of $3,500,000.
As mentioned, it is intended that the new line will connect with the existing system of pipe lines commonly known as the Canol project. This Canol project consists of a 3-inch line from Whitehorse to the Yukon-Alaska border parallel to the Alaska highway and, in addition, a 2-inch pipe line extending from Carcross, Yukon, to Watson Lake at mile 634 on the Alaska highway, a length of almost 300 miles.
I should explain that the Canol system of pipe lines was constructed during the second world war by the United States government with the consent, of course, of the Canadian government. It was constructed for the purpose of transporting petroleum products for the use of army and air force establishments in the north during the war. It is understood that the 3-inch and 2-inch lines are shortly to be deactivated and declared surplus by the United States government.
The people of the world today are more aware than ever before of the tremendously important role performed by oil and oil products in providing fuel for heating, power, and lubrication to keep the wheels of modern industry turning. This is just as applicable to the economy of the north as it is in other parts of Canada and the world. In the Alaska-Yukon area the point that stands out most clearly is the lack of basic industry to create new wealth through the utilization of natural resources in the region. The development of these resources is the firm basis for sound and stable growth.
The main requirement for prosperous business and living conditions may be summed up in one word, "oil". Whether it be transportation, highway construction, or heating of homes, hospitals, churches and places of industry, the need for oil and oil products is a paramount one. As a major contribution to the solution of this problem in the northwest part of this continent, Alaska-Yukon Refiners and Distributors Limited propose to enter aggressively into the business of refining, transporting and distributing petroleum products in both the Yukon and Alaska.

It is proposed to accomplish this in two main ways. It is planned to construct a 6,500 to 10,000 barrel per day refinery at Haines, Alaska, at a cost of $6 million to $10 million. The measure before the house has reference to the other aspect of the project, namely the building and operating of pipe lines by Alaska-Yukon Pipelines Limited. At a later stage in this entire development it is planned to build a line also from Tok Junction near the Alaska border to Anchorage in Alaska, at an estimated cost of between $5 million and $6 million.
The bill before the house has already been examined carefully in the other place and has been passed with only one alteration in its original form. The only change is the broadening of the geographical scope of the bill in order to meet any possible special conditions that may arise in the future in the north in the way of oil developments.
I wish to explain also that no shares of this company are being offered in the United States of America. The financing operations will be carried out entirely within Canada. Alaska-Yukon Refiners and Distributors Limited is incorporated under the laws of Alberta, and the head office will be in Edmonton. The directors are men well trained in the industry and experienced in the operation of facilities for handling distributing and marketing petroleum products.
In view of the way the economy of the Yukon Territory and Alaska is expanding, economists who are trained in making business analyses and in judging business trends claim that the project envisioned by this company will be of great economic benefit to the north generally. Industrial enterprise is urgently needed in that region, and this particular project is certain to be a major factor in establishing industrial incentives.
For the entire lifetime of the north country, and this is true of both the Yukon and Alaska, practically all petroleum requirements have been filled from California sources. This supply has been in the nature of a monopoly. The addition of a modern refinery and the entry of another distributing company will be warmly welcomed and supported by the people of both territories. I firmly believe that this project fits strategically within the present era of prosperity and development throughout Canada. Moreover, it is in the competent hands of those who know the north and its needs, as well as its challenging opportunities.
Once the necessary legislative authority is granted I know an early start will be made on pipe-line construction. Pipe is on order at the present time, and it is hoped that the

building of the line will commence early in May of this year and be completed as far as Haines Junction by late September or early October.
When the bill is given second reading in this chamber, any hon. member wishing to raise a particular point concerning the measure will have an opportunity to do so in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Mr. Speaker, while listening to the mellifluous and dulcet tones of the hon. member for Yukon during his interesting recitation of the virtues of this bill, my mind wandered back to the early days of this century. As a matter of fact, it was only recently that I was in a hall where the hon. member made his first speech in 1904. On that occasion he was rewarded with an all-day sucker. Today he expects to be rewarded by the passage of this bill. However, I can assure the hon. member that his reward will not be as prompt on this occasion as it was on the occasion of his first speech.
I listened with interest to the hon. member's lucid explanation of the purpose of the bill and the intention of the company. While necessarily we have to reserve judgment at this stage, I was pleased to learn that no shares are being offered in the United States. That is like a breath of fresh air. I was also glad to learn that as a result the company will be Canadian-owned.
I am quite sure the hon. member realizes what the pipe line will mean to the Yukon country when he said it would be a major factor in promoting industrial development in the region he has the honour to represent. I was also interested in another comment he made. He suggested, if I heard him correctly, that at the present time the people of the Yukon suffer somewhat from monopoly conditions in connection with the distribution of oil, and that with the building of the pipe line and the consequent refinery that condition would change and some competition would be provided for the present distributors in the area.
However, as a Canadian I have, on the surface at least, one serious objection at the present time to the bill. Excuse me, Mr. Speaker, but my colleague has got my literature mixed up with his rubbish. The title of the bill is "An act to incorporate Alaska-Yukon Pipelines Limited". In view of the fact that the hon. member tells us that all the stock will be subscribed for in Canada, that in effect it will be a Canadian company and that its major purpose is to serve the needs and requirements of the people of the

Private Bills
Yukon and the future industrial development, I think it is most unfortunate that the name of the company should be "Alaska-Yukon Pipelines Limited." I suggest to the hon. member that when we get in committee we will do all we can to have the title changed to Yukon-Alaska Pipelines Limited, which would more correctly describe the objectives and purposes of the company.
It is very difficult to pass judgment on a bill of this nature without it being referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and I was very pleased to hear the hon. member say the bill is going to that committee. I hope the committee will have the opportunity to question witnesses, commencing with the hon. member himself, who I am sure will have a fund of valuable information to give the committee, and also officials of the company concerned and possibly some engineers and other persons with technical knowledge and experience.
Having said these few things in connection with the bill, Mr. Speaker, we reserve our judgment on it until we have heard and examined the witnesses in the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I hope when the hon. member for Yukon closes the debate he will see fit to inform the house what the precise role was that was being played by the hon. member for Kootenay West at the time the member for Yukon got an all-day sucker. I join with my colleague, the member for Kootenay West, in appreciating the interest the member for Yukon has in seeing developments take place in his part of the country, and I was interested in his outline of the development that he envisages will take place if this bill is passed by the house. More and more those of us who have not yet had the opportunity of seeing firsthand the part of the country from which he comes are becoming interested in it and in its welfare and development.
However, there are one or two points which I think should come to our minds in relation to what the hon. member said when introducing the bill. If I caught his words correctly he said that the bill in its present form and substance follows the same pattern as previous pipe-line bills which have been introduced in and approved by the house. In view of some of the developments which have been brought to our attention recently in respect of pipe-line companies that have been incorporated under bills of this type, we cannot help having some misgivings with respect to bills that follow this pattern as this one does and as those will which may come up in the future.
I appreciate the interest the hon. member has in seeing his part of the country develop.
[Mr. Herridge.l
However, I notice that this company is going to start its organization having in its treasury one million shares of nominal par value. I cannot help but wonder whether in the course of time the same situation will develop in the hon. member's part of the country that has developed in British Columbia, where we see pipe-line companies that were incorporated a few years ago in a similar manner providing lucrative returns to their promoters at the expense of those who are going to rely on the facilities created.
These questions arise in my mind as I consider the matter of approving the principle of the bill which the hon. member is introducing. I hope when we get into the committee those witnesses to- whom the hon. member for Kootenay West referred will appear and give us assurances that are more convincing than those given by witnesses who have appeared on previous occasions when bills of this type were being considered. I hope they will be able to convince us that they are not looking for the kind of concessions that others apparently have been able to get. Perhaps they may have some explanation to offer as to the intention in respect to issuing shares or options on shares to directors and that sort of thing.
If the hon. member is in a position to give us some assurances of that kind when he closes the debate on second reading of course we will be very glad to receive them; but as the hon. member for Kootenay West said, we are perhaps prepared to reserve any real judgment on this matter until the bill has been discussed in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
I think I really do not need to explain to the hon. member for Yukon and this house that as far as we in the C.C.F. group are concerned we would much prefer to see this initiative taken in his part of the country as a public venture, under which all the benefits of the pipe-line transmission would accrue to the users of the facilities, those who will be dependent on them.
I shall not say any more on that subject at this time. If the hon. member cares to give us any assurances in this respect when he closes the debate, we will be glad to have them, as I have said. Otherwise we may have some questions to ask when the bill reaches the committee stage.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with respect to Bill No. 177. I want to make it clear that I have no objection to the passing of Bill No. 177, which is a little different from most of the bills in this category. In this case the petitioner has asked not for a divorce but rather for an annulment. I think anyone who might read the evidence would agree that an annulment in this case is appropriate. However, it does seem to me that a rather grievous error in the permanent records of parliament has occurred which should be corrected. I am not sure just how it can be done, but I will lay the matter before Your Honour and perhaps you might find a solution.
In reading through the evidence in connection with this case it is thoroughly and abundantly clear that there is no question of adultery on anyone's part. The reason for the request for the annulment is non-consummation. It is clear in the evidence that the man and the wife in this case lived together for six or seven years and that every effort was made to achieve harmonious and normal relations. I do not think I need say anything further about the evidence. It is well stated, well given, and the witnesses included medical men. So far as the evidence is concerned everything is quite satisfactory.
However, when one looks at page 6 of the report of the committee on divorce in the other place regarding this case he finds this paragraph over the name of the clerk of the Senate subcommittee, also with the word "attest" at the left side. This is the paragraph:
It was resolved to report to the main committee that: Your subcommittee find as a fact that, according to the evidence adduced, the allegations contained in paragraphs 6 to 8, both inclusive and particularly that the respondent committed adultery as alleged in paragraphs 6 and 6a of the said petition, have been proved.
There is no reference in paragraphs 6 to 8, Mr. Speaker, particularly there is no reference in paragraphs 6 and 6a of the petition
Private Bills-Divorce
to adultery; there is no reference to adultery anywhere in the evidence concerning this case, yet the subcommittee reported to the main committee of the other place that a divorce should be granted on the basis of adultery having been proved.
I have pursued this matter a little further so far as the records of the other place are concerned, and I find that the report of this case was the 158th report of the committee on divorce and that it was made in the other place on February 7 by Senator Roebuck. It reads, as recorded in the Votes and Proceedings of the Senate, as follows:
With respect to the petition of . . . for an act to dissolve his marriage with . . .
I do not think I need to read any more. I checked on this and I find that whenever an annulment is requested and put through parliament the wording is different. Instead of the words "to dissolve" the report uses the words "to annul". The actual bill that is before us is correct. The bill, namely No. 177, varies from the rest of the bills we have in that instead of stating in clause 1 that the marriage is hereby dissolved it says, "the marriage is hereby annulled." The preamble is correct; the bill is correct.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that in the official records of the other place, and I include such records in the records of parliament, there is a gross misstatement in that the lady in this case is accused of having committed adultery and it is alleged in these reports that this fact has been proved. It was not alleged; it is not in the petition; there is no reference to it in the evidence at all. It is a clear case of non-consummation despite the attempt on the part of husband and wife to live together harmoniously and normally for six or seven years, and I would hope Your Honour might find some way, either when the report is made to return this evidence to the other place or in some other way open to Your Honour, to have the record of the other place corrected so there will not be on the permanent records of parliament an allegation of adultery said to be proved against a person in an instance where such an allegation is absolutely false.
I have no objection to the bill; I think it should be passed. I would hope, however, that a way might be found to correct this error in the records of the other place.
